pages.title: How is this learning path structured
pages.content:
Welcome to the Beginner's path to solving programming problems.
- Getting started, Basic math and Conditional statements are introductory modules.\
If you are well versed in these topics - feel free to skip to the module on [Logic building](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/python-beginner-v2-p1/BP00BP12_V2/problems/LB00)
- Logic building covers our **5-step approach** to solving programming problems
- Array operations, String operations and Basic math continued will require patience, hard-work and heavy-lifting. If you want to directly start with these - click [here](https://www.codechef.com/learn/python-beginner-v2-p2)

How should you approach this learning path?
- Within each module - there are multiple topics. 
- You will be able to finish each topic in 30 - 45 mins
- Each topic consists of the following to ensure that you **Learn by doing**
  - Concept problems introduce new syntax, concepts and methods
  - Practice and Debugging problems require you to solve problems yourself
- At the end of each module, you have Review problems. 

Best of luck for your programming journey ahead! \
Click on 'Next' to proceed.

pages.title: Getting started with programming problems
pages.content:
If you are here - then you already know the [basic syntax of Python](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/python).\
Let's now take it up a notch and train you to solve programming problems.

On SEED-IT and other platforms, you will come across programming problems.
- Each programming problem has a **problem statement**
- You write a **solution code** which will solve the problem
- Your code is run, does some computation and generates **your output**
- **Your output** is compared with the **Expected output**. 
  - If they match - then your code is correct!
  - If they don't match - then there is some error in your code.

Click on **Next** to proceed!

practiceProblems.title: How to accept inputs
practiceProblems.description:
Ok - so let us begin your journey.

For solving programming problems, your code needs to accept system provided inputs. \
The $input()$ function in **Python** allows user input.
- The default parameter accepted in the $input()$ function is a string
- All values entered using `input()` are treated as strings, even if they look like numbers.

### Task
Write a code to accept a string as input and output the same. \
Some portion of the code is already written for you. \
You need to replace the _ (underscores) with correct code in the editor. \
Once done, click **Submit**.

Note: We learned about all the basic concepts of Python in [Learn Python Path](https://www.codechef.com/learn/python). You should finish it first if you are unsure of the syntax.

practiceProblems.title: How to accept multiple inputs in a line
practiceProblems.description:
Sometimes we have to accept multiple inputs in a single line.

The way to accept multiple integers in a single line is to use the **split** and **map** function.

- **split** function breaks the input based on the separator - by default, it splits inputs separated by spaces in a single line into different inputs which you can assign to different variables
- **map** function converts each input into the defined datatype

The syntax for the same is as follows -
```python
a, b, c = map(int, input().split())   # assigns integer input values to variables a, b and c

# In this code, we take input using input(), then split it using input().split().
# Once the input is split, we convert each value into a integer using map.
```



### Task
Now lets try and solve the following
- Accept 3 space separated integers given in a line into 3 variables - $A$, $B$ and $C$
- Print them out to a single line on the console

Code the solution in the IDE and then click **Submit** to continue.

pages.title: What are custom inputs
pages.content:
What are custom inputs? \
You will usually find a 'custom' inputs box in programming problems. 

**Custom** inputs allow you to do the following
- You are able to see the output generated by your code for inputs defined by you
- Test your code with your sample inputs.\
This helps you debug the following errors faster
```python
Wrong Answers (WA)
Runtime Errors (RE)
```
- Create your own **test cases**. \
In programming problems - you want to find exceptions or test cases where your code / logic can fail. \
**Custom** inputs allow you to test your code for the same.

Click on **Next** to proceed.

- Once done, click on **Submit** to test your code against the **Private test files**

practiceProblems.title: Difference between Run and Submit
practiceProblems.description:
What is the difference between the **Run** and **Submit** buttons?
- **Run** allows you to locally test your code on **sample inputs** and **custom inputs**
   - Custom inputs are small inputs - mainly for you to test your code
- **Submit** sends your code to the online judge to compare your **Actual output** and the **Expected output**
   - On submission - your code is checked against thousands of test cases which are included in the **hidden** or **private** test files
   - Your code / solution is complete only when you click **Submit** and get an **AC** (accepted) verdict
   - **Note:** Your code can run as expected for your custom inputs - however, it can fail on the **private** test files. \
This means your code is **NOT** solving the problem correctly and needs to be fixed.



### Task

- Accepts the count of test cases - $t$ - in the 1st line. \
First line of each test case consists of an integer $N$
- Outputs the integer which is greater than $N$ by $1$
- Click on **Run** to check the result on custom inputs
- Click on **Submit** to check the final verdict
